contract: Implement `fieldreport.py`. A report is assembled from titled sections containing paragraphs, measurements, warnings, source references, and images (image data is only a path and alt text). It must render deterministic plain text, HTML, and JSON. Each render selects an audience clearance; material above it is omitted, but a section whose body disappears must not leave an empty heading. References are numbered in first-use order in the rendered result, repeated references reuse a number, and broken references are reported before rendering. HTML must escape user text; JSON must retain measurement value/unit separately. Provide `Report`, `validate(report)`, and `render(report, format, clearance)`. Executable acceptance contract: Build one report with two sections, a shared source, `` text, a public paragraph and restricted warning. Assert exact public/admin text; `html.escape` behavior; `json.loads` has separate measurement fields; shared citation is `[1]`; hidden-only heading is absent; and `validate` returns a stable missing-source diagnostic. Also build the same report in two processes with different hash seeds and compare output. Use only the Python standard library. Public API and data-format contract (the implementation's internal organization is unrestricted): `Report(sections, sources)` accepts `sections` as a list of dictionaries and `sources` as a mapping from source ID to `{"title": str, "url": str}`. Each section is `{"title": str, "items": list}`. Each item has `kind` (`paragraph`, `measurement`, `warning`, `reference`, or `image`), optional `clearance` (`public` by default or `admin`), and these fields: paragraph/warning: `text`; measurement: `label`, `value`, `unit`; reference: `source`, `text`; image: `path`, `alt`. Inputs must not be mutated. `validate(report)` returns a sorted list of strings, with a missing source reported exactly as `missing source: `. `render(report, format, clearance)` accepts format `text`, `html`, or `json`, and clearance `public` or `admin`; unknown values raise `ValueError`. A section is omitted when none of its items are visible. In text, sections use `## `, paragraph text is literal, measurements use `<label>: <value> <unit>`, warnings use `WARNING: <text>`, references use `<text> [n]`, and images use `[Image: <alt>] (<path>)`; nonempty sections and the final reference list are separated by one blank line. The reference list is headed `References:` and entries are `[n] <title> — <url>`. There is no reference-list block if none are used, and the result has no trailing newline. HTML is one `<section><h2>...</h2>...</section>` per included section; item elements are respectively `<p>`, `<p class="measurement" data-unit="..."><strong>label:</strong> value unit</p>`, `<p class="warning">`, `<p class="reference">text <a href="url">[n]</a></p>`, and `<img src="path" alt="alt">`. If used, references are an `<ol class="references">` whose `<li>` elements contain linked titles. All user-provided strings, including attributes, are escaped with `html.escape(..., quote=True)`. JSON is a deterministic JSON object with keys `sections` and `references`; each included section has `title` and `items`, and each item retains its kind-specific fields (a measurement retains separate `value` and `unit`); reference items additionally contain integer `number`. `references` is a first-use-ordered list of objects with `number`, `id`, `title`, and `url`. JSON must parse with `json.loads` and deterministic rendering uses stable key ordering.
notes: Covers both clearances, empty-section suppression, exact text, escaping, typed JSON measurements, citation reuse/first-use order, diagnostics, immutability, invalid choices, and cross-process hash-seed determinism.

contract:
Implement `access.py`. A request supplies person attributes, entrance, local timestamp, and requested activity. Requirements may allow or deny based on badge class, training expiry, escort presence, weekday/time window, temporary closure, and emergency mode. The service returns allow/deny plus an ordered explanation containing every requirement that affected the answer. It must evaluate one request, evaluate a batch, list which currently configured requirements would change their answer if emergency mode toggled, and support a dry evaluation with one hypothetical attribute replacement. Requirement order in configuration must not change the answer or explanation.

Executable acceptance contract: Fixed `datetime` cases cover expired training, overnight windows, simultaneous closure and missing escort, emergency override, batch equivalence to scalar calls, hypothetical badge replacement without mutation, permutation-invariant explanations, and precise “affected by emergency” listing. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (the implementation's internal organization is unrestricted):
Provide `AccessService(requirements)`. Requirements are dictionaries with a unique string `id`, a `type`, and type-specific fields. Supported forms are: `{"type":"badge", "allowed":[...]}`, `{"type":"training", "name":...}` (the request's `training` mapping holds expiry datetimes and the expiry is valid when it is at or after the request timestamp), `{"type":"escort"}`, `{"type":"window", "weekdays":[0..6], "start":"HH:MM", "end":"HH:MM"}` (equal endpoints mean all day; an end earlier than start is overnight and its after-midnight part belongs to the preceding allowed weekday), `{"type":"closure", "start":datetime, "end":datetime}` (inclusive start, exclusive end), and `{"type":"emergency_override", "overrides":[requirement IDs...]}`. Request dictionaries contain `badge`, `training`, `escort` (bool), `entrance`, `timestamp`, and `activity`; inputs are not mutated.
`evaluate(request, emergency=False)` returns `{"allowed": bool, "explanation": list[str]}`. Each failed applicable non-override requirement contributes `<id>: <message>` where messages are respectively `badge not allowed`, `training <name> expired or missing`, `escort required`, `outside access window`, and `temporarily closed`. In emergency mode, an emergency-override requirement makes its named failures non-blocking and contributes `<override-id>: emergency override of <comma-separated sorted failed IDs>`; the overridden failure messages are not included. Explanations are sorted by requirement ID, making configuration permutations immaterial. `evaluate_batch(requests, emergency=False)` equals scalar evaluation in input order. `evaluate_with(request, replacements, emergency=False)` evaluates a shallow request copy updated by `replacements`. `affected_by_emergency(request)` returns the sorted requirement IDs whose own blocking/non-blocking effect changes between modes (the failed IDs that an applicable emergency override names), not the override requirement's ID.
notes: Uses fixed datetimes for inclusive expiry, overnight weekday semantics, simultaneous denials, override effects, scalar/batch parity, dry replacement, ordering invariance, and input immutability.

contract:
Implement `settings.py`. Combine defaults, a project file, an optional user file, environment-style strings, and explicit call arguments. Nested mappings merge; a value can explicitly remove an inherited key; lists replace rather than merge. Convert declared fields to bool, integer, `Path`, or comma-separated strings. Report all conversion and unknown-key problems together. A caller can ask for the final value of a dotted key and an explanation showing where each candidate came from, including removed and invalid candidates, without exposing secrets. The inputs must not be mutated.

Executable acceptance contract: Plain dictionaries test nested merge, deletion sentinel, list replacement, false-like strings, `pathlib.Path`, three simultaneous errors, secret masking in explanations, provenance order, absent key, and deep-copy equality of all inputs afterward. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (the implementation's internal organization is unrestricted):
Expose the string constant `DELETE = "__DELETE__"` and `load(defaults, project, user, environ, explicit, schema, secrets=())`. The first three and `explicit` are nested dictionaries (`user` may be `None`); `environ` is a dictionary whose dotted keys identify settings; source precedence, low to high, is defaults, project, user, environ, explicit. Nested mappings merge, lists replace, and a value equal to `DELETE` removes that key and its descendants. `schema` maps dotted keys to one of `"bool"`, `"int"`, `"path"`, `"csv"`, `"str"`, `"list"`, or `"mapping"`. Environment values and other scalar candidates for declared fields are converted: bool accepts case-insensitive `true/yes/on/1` and `false/no/off/0`; int uses base-10; path produces `pathlib.Path`; csv splits on commas and strips each part; str requires a string. `list` and `mapping` require those types. Keys absent from `schema` (except prefixes of declared dotted keys) are unknown. All unknown-key and conversion errors are accumulated, sorted, and do not raise.
`load` returns an object with attributes `data` (the successfully resolved nested dictionary) and `errors` (list of strings), and methods `get(dotted_key, default=None)` and `explain(dotted_key)`. Errors are exactly `unknown key <dotted>` or `invalid <dotted> from <source>: expected <type>`, where source is `defaults`, `project`, `user`, `environ`, or `explicit`. An invalid candidate does not replace the last valid value. `explain` returns candidates in source precedence order as a list of dictionaries with `source`, `status` (`selected`, `overridden`, `removed`, or `invalid`), and `value`. Only candidates actually supplied for that key are listed. For keys in `secrets`, every explanation value other than `None` is the literal `"***"`, including invalid and removed candidates. An absent key explains as `[]`. Neither arguments nor nested contents may be mutated.
notes: Covers recursive overlay, deletion, replacement lists, conversions, accumulated errors, invalid fallback, provenance statuses/order, secret masking, absent lookup, and deep input immutability.

contract:
Implement `oralhistory.py`. Store transcript segments with speaker, time range, text, and stable ID. Editors can correct text, split a segment, join adjacent segments, attach topic tags and source notes, and mark private spans within a segment. Existing notes and external links to a segment must remain resolvable after splits and joins. Export public and researcher transcripts, a speaker index, a topic index, and a revision comparison. Public output replaces private words with one marker while retaining useful timing. Concurrent edit branches may be combined when they touch disjoint material; otherwise return a readable conflict.

Executable acceptance contract: Build a small transcript, link a note, split and join, assert link resolution and tag inheritance, redaction, indexes, comparison, branch merge of disjoint corrections, conflict on the same text, stable ordering, and immutability of base revision. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (the implementation's internal organization is unrestricted):
Provide `Workspace(segments)` where every segment dictionary has `id`, `speaker`, `start`, `end`, `text`, `tags` (a list), and `private` (a list of `[start_offset, end_offset]` pairs using Python string offsets). Segment IDs are unique and output ordering is by `(start, end, id)`. The following methods return a workspace containing the edit and leave their receiver and all caller inputs unchanged: `correct(id, text)`, `split(id, offset, left_id, right_id)`, `join(left_id, right_id, joined_id)`, `add_tag(id, tag)`, `mark_private(id, start, end)`, `add_note(note_id, segment_id, text)`, and `add_link(link_id, segment_id, url)`. Split requires `0 < offset < len(text)`, divides timing linearly, clips/rebases private spans, and copies tags to both results. Join requires adjacent segments in workspace order, the same speaker, and `left.end == right.start`; it concatenates text with one space, unions tags, and shifts right private offsets by `len(left.text)+1`.
`notes()` returns note dictionaries sorted by note ID, each with `id`, `text`, and `segments` listing the current segment IDs to which the note applies. `links()` does the same for external links, with dictionaries containing `id`, `url`, and `segments`. If an attached segment is split, its note/link applies to both resulting segments; if attached material is joined, its note/link applies to the joined segment. These results are required only through `notes()` and `links()`; no additional lookup API is required.
`export(clearance)` returns lines `<start>-<end> <speaker>: <text>` joined by newlines in segment order; clearance is `public` or `researcher`. Public text replaces each maximal private span with exactly `[PRIVATE]`; researcher text is unchanged. `speaker_index()` and `topic_index()` return dictionaries mapping speaker/tag to ordered current segment-ID lists. `compare(other)` returns a list of strings, sorted by segment ID, in the exact forms `added <id>`, `removed <id>`, or `changed <id>` (an ID present in both but with unequal segment data).
`merge(base, left, right)` combines two edited workspaces when their only edits are `correct` and/or `add_tag`: changes to different segment IDs, or a text correction on one side and tag additions on the other side of the same ID, combine; differing text corrections to the same ID raise publicly importable `ConflictError` whose string is `conflict on <id>: text`.
notes: Revised after semantic audit. Tests only current transcript, attachment, export, index, comparison, merge, conflict, ordering, and non-mutation behavior. There is no public lookup for superseded IDs and no exposed revision representation.
leakage_self_audit: The appended contract specifies only constructor inputs, edit calls, current observable outputs, comparison results, and conflict behavior. Attachment continuity is checked through current notes/links rather than through a general identity-resolution API. Full copied workspaces, repair tables, replayed edits, or other materially different internals can satisfy it; no internal organization is named or behaviorally required.

contract:
Implement `labels.py`. An exhibit label contains a title, creator names, date ranges, dimensions, narrative paragraphs, quoted text, and credit lines. Generate labels for locales `en`, `fr`, and `ja`, for wall, mobile, and accessible-audio uses. Locale changes punctuation, name order, number/date presentation, and available translations; use the supplied translation dictionary only. Missing translations fall back to source text but must be reported. Mobile has a length budget and may omit optional paragraphs; credit lines may never be omitted. Accessible audio must verbalize symbols and image descriptions. Return output plus omissions/fallbacks.

Executable acceptance contract: Fixed fixture asserts exact name/date/dimension presentation per locale, quote punctuation, mobile optional omission but retained credit, audio symbol expansion, fallback diagnostics, deterministic output, and no calls to locale/global environment (tests can patch `locale.setlocale` to fail). Use only the Python standard library.

Public API/data-format contract: `generate_label(exhibit, locale, use, mobile_budget=None) -> dict`. Inputs and outputs are JSON-shaped values. `exhibit` has `title`, `creators` (each `{given,family}`), `date` (`{start,end}` ISO dates, with equal dates allowed), `dimensions_cm` (`[height,width]` numbers), `paragraphs` (each `{id,text,optional}`), `quotes` (strings), `credits` (strings), `image_descriptions` (strings), and `translations`, a mapping from locale to a mapping from source string to translated string. `locale` is `en`, `fr`, or `ja`; `use` is `wall`, `mobile`, or `audio`. The result is `{text, omissions, fallbacks}`, where the latter two are sorted lists of source paragraph IDs and untranslated source strings. Translation is looked up independently for every title, paragraph, quote, credit, and image description; `en` source strings need no dictionary entry. Names render “given family” in en/fr and “family given” in ja. Dates render `YYYY-MM-DD` in en, `DD/MM/YYYY` in fr, and `YYYY年M月D日` in ja; a range joins with `–`, while equal endpoints render once. Dimensions render `H × W cm` in en/fr and `H × W cm` in ja, using ordinary decimal text without trailing `.0`. Quotes use “…” in en, « … » in fr, and 「…」 in ja. A non-audio label consists, in order, of title, creators joined by `, `, date, dimensions, included paragraphs, quotes, and credits, joined by newline. For mobile, repeatedly omit optional paragraphs from the end until UTF-8-decoded character length is at most `mobile_budget`; if mandatory content alone exceeds the budget, return it unchanged. Credits are mandatory. Audio has no budget or omissions and joins the same fields plus image descriptions by newline, but replaces `&`, `×`, and `%` in all rendered text with locale words (`and/times/percent`, `et/fois/pour cent`, `と/かける/パーセント`). Invalid locale/use raises `ValueError`. The function must not mutate its input.
notes: In-memory fixture covers every locale and medium across assertions, exact punctuation/formatting, fallback, omission, accessibility expansion, determinism, mutation, invalid input, and locale-global isolation.
leakage_self_audit: No forbidden terms occur. Contract fixes only callable/schema and observable formatting, lookup, budget, diagnostics, error, and purity rules; it does not prescribe how locale and use handling are organized.

contract:
Implement `survey.py`. Import observation rows from supplied CSV text and JSON objects. Observations include observer, local time with explicit UTC offset, location, species label, count, optional photo hash, and notes. Produce a canonical export, daily/site/species summaries, possible-duplicate groups, and a reconciliation report. Exact photo matches are duplicates; otherwise records are only “possible” duplicates when supplied tolerances for time and coordinates and compatible species aliases hold. Staff may decide that a group is same or distinct, and future imports must honor that decision. Preserve original spellings and rows for audit.

Executable acceptance contract: Use `csv`, `json`, and `datetime`; cover offsets crossing UTC date, aliases, exact hash duplicate, near-but-not-certain pair, persisted same/distinct decisions, summaries before/after reconciliation, stable canonical export under import order reversal, and original-row recovery. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API/data-format contract: Provide class `Survey(time_tolerance_seconds, coordinate_tolerance)`. `import_csv(text)` accepts columns `id,observer,local_time,latitude,longitude,species,count,photo_hash,notes`; `import_json(rows)` accepts equivalent dicts. IDs are nonempty and unique. Local times are ISO-8601 strings with explicit offsets. The object exposes `possible_duplicates() -> list[dict]`, `decide(member_ids, decision)`, `summaries() -> dict`, `canonical_export() -> str`, `reconciliation_report() -> dict`, and `original_row(id) -> dict`. A duplicate group dict is `{group_id,members,reason}` with sorted member IDs; `reason` is `photo` for equal nonempty hashes and otherwise `possible`. Its `group_id` is the first 16 lowercase hex characters of SHA-256 over comma-joined sorted member IDs. Non-photo pairs qualify only if absolute UTC-time difference is within the supplied inclusive tolerance, Euclidean latitude/longitude distance is within the supplied inclusive tolerance, and their species labels are compatible. Species aliases are supplied by `set_aliases(mapping)`, where each key maps to a list including all compatible spellings; matching is case-insensitive, but original spelling is retained. `decide` accepts exactly a currently reported member list and `same` or `distinct`; decisions survive later imports. `same` collapses those observations to one resolved observation for summaries, using the lexicographically smallest ID as representative; `distinct` prevents that exact group from being reported or collapsed. Exact equal hashes collapse unless explicitly decided distinct. Summaries returns `{daily,site,species}` maps of summed counts keyed respectively by UTC date, `"latitude,longitude"` using input decimal text, and representative original species spelling. Each collapsed group contributes the maximum member count. Canonical export is compact JSON (`sort_keys=True`, separators `(',',':')`) containing observations sorted by ID and decisions sorted by member list, and is independent of import order. The report is `{groups,decisions}` in deterministic group/member order. `original_row` returns all originally supplied field strings (JSON numeric values converted to their input `str` form) and a `source` key (`csv` or `json`). No method mutates returned values.
notes: Exercises CSV and JSON ingestion, UTC-day crossing, aliases, exact and possible duplicates, durable same/distinct decisions after later import, summaries, stable export, and audit recovery.
leakage_self_audit: No forbidden terms occur. Although stable group IDs and representative/count rules are necessary to make outputs executable, storage and reconciliation implementation remain unconstrained (tables, copies, flags, objects, or procedures all fit).

contract:
Implement `recipebook.py`. Recipes contain ingredient quantities, preparation statements referring to ingredients, equipment needs, yields, and optional components. Adapt a recipe to a target yield, available equipment, dietary exclusions, and a supplied substitution catalog. Substitutions may change quantity, unit, preparation wording, equipment, or yield and may introduce another excluded ingredient. Return the adapted recipe, all applied choices and warnings, or all reasons no adaptation is possible. Original recipes remain printable exactly as authored. Units use rational quantities; do not depend on a unit package.

Executable acceptance contract: With `fractions.Fraction`, test scaling 3→5 servings, chained substitution, substitution changing a referenced verb and equipment, detection of an exclusion reintroduced later, multiple simultaneous impossibility reasons, exact original print after adaptations, and deterministic choice using explicit catalog priority. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API/data-format contract: `adapt(recipe, request, catalog) -> dict` and `print_original(recipe) -> str`. Quantities and yields are `fractions.Fraction`; other values are JSON-shaped. A recipe has `{title,yield,ingredients,equipment,instructions,components,authored_text}`. Each ingredient is `{id,name,quantity,unit,preparation}`. `instructions` is a list of plain authored strings; it contains no mandatory reference keys or links. `request` is `{target_yield,available_equipment,excluded}`. Each catalog choice has `{id,for,priority,result}`; `result` describes a replacement ingredient (`name`, and optional `quantity_factor`, `unit`, `preparation`), optional `wording_changes` pairs `{old,new}`, optional equipment additions/removals, and optional additional ingredients. Lower numeric priority wins, with catalog order as the tie-breaker. The returned value is `{possible,recipe,choices,warnings,reasons}`. If possible, `recipe` is a complete adapted recipe at the target yield, all quantities reflect the yield change and selected replacement factors, no excluded ingredient remains anywhere, its equipment is sorted and contained in `available_equipment`, selected wording changes are reflected in the final instruction strings, and `reasons` is empty. `choices` is the ordered list of chosen catalog IDs and `warnings` is sorted. If impossible, `recipe` is null and `reasons` is a sorted list containing every independently applicable reason, not merely the first; reason text is `no substitution for NAME`, `equipment NAME unavailable`, or `substitution cycle involving NAME`. `choices` may describe choices considered before impossibility was established. Additional ingredients are subject to the same exclusions and catalog choices, so chained adaptations are supported. `print_original` returns `authored_text` byte-for-byte as a Python string. Neither function may mutate its inputs. Only final observable wording is specified: implementations may use direct text edits, positional indexes, richer private objects, regeneration, search, or any other organization.
notes: Second semantic revision removes all mandatory instruction-to-ingredient references. Instructions are plain strings; the test asserts only final observable wording, scaling, choices, equipment, failures, authored printing, determinism, and purity.
leakage_self_audit: No forbidden term occurs. Public instructions carry neither ingredient IDs nor links. Wording changes describe only required final text. Direct string editing, positional indexing, private semantic objects, template regeneration, search, and other organizations can all satisfy the contract; no internal sequencing or linked representation is observable.

contract:
Implement `meeting.py`. An agenda has numbered items, nested subitems, presenters, supporting documents, expected durations, consent-group membership, and private staff notes. During the meeting, record reorderings, withdrawals, motions, votes, recesses, and actual timestamps. Produce the pre-meeting public agenda, chair’s run sheet, final minutes, action-item register, and a comparison of planned versus actual sequence and duration. Original item numbers remain valid references after reorder or withdrawal. Invalid events must be reported together rather than stopping at the first.

Executable acceptance contract: Use fixed datetimes; create nested items and consent group, reorder and withdraw one, record motion/roll-call/tie and recess; assert all five exact views, stable original references, duration comparison, action extraction, and aggregation of a bad item reference plus impossible event order. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API/data-format contract: Provide `Meeting(agenda)`. The agenda is `{meeting_id,start,items,consent_groups}` using `datetime.datetime` values; items are recursive `{number,title,presenter,documents,expected_minutes,private_notes,subitems,action}` dicts, and original `number` strings are unique permanent references. The object accepts calls `reorder(order, at)`, `withdraw(item, at)`, `add_motion(item, text, at) -> motion_ref`, `record_vote(item, motion_ref, votes, at)`, and `add_recess(start, end)`. Votes map member names to `yes`, `no`, or `abstain`. Calls do not raise for meeting-data errors; they accumulate them. `documents() -> dict` returns exactly `{public_agenda,chair_run_sheet,minutes,actions,comparison,errors}` and may be called repeatedly without changing the result. Public agenda is the original recursive agenda without private notes/actions. Chair run sheet adds private notes and consent-group name or null. Minutes is a chronological list with exact entry shapes: reorder `{type:'reorder',order,at}`, withdrawal `{type:'withdraw',item,at}`, motion `{type:'motion',item,text,ref,at}`, vote `{type:'vote',item,ref,votes,result,at}`, and recess `{type:'recess',minutes,at}`. Datetimes render as ISO text; vote result is `passed`, `failed`, or `tie` after excluding abstentions, and recess minutes are integers. Actions is sorted `{item,action}` entries for nonwithdrawn items. Comparison has one row per top-level planned item: `{item,planned_position,actual_position,expected_minutes,actual_minutes,status}`; withdrawn position is null, and status is `withdrawn`, `moved`, or `as_planned`. Actual minutes run from the first proceeding for an item until the next proceeding for a different item or the last proceeding, less recess overlap; an item with none has zero. Errors are sorted and include all applicable `unknown item X`, `timestamps out of order`, `recess ends before it starts`, and `invalid reorder`; invalid calls do not alter the five document views. Inputs are not mutated. The API does not constrain whether an implementation annotates agenda copies, keeps parallel state, uses commands, snapshots, or another design.
notes: Revised to an imperative meeting object receiving clerk operations, rather than a public event-sequence value. Tests assert all five exact documents, stable references, timing/action behavior, idempotence, and accumulated invalid-call diagnostics.
leakage_self_audit: No forbidden term occurs. There is no public sequence container or replay API. Individual clerk calls and document results can be implemented by annotating copies, parallel planned/actual state, snapshots, commands, or other organizations; chronological minutes are required domain output only.

contract:
Implement `approval.py`. Packaging assets have regions (front, back, side), text claims, colors, images, and supplied checksum. Reviewers in legal, brand, and accessibility can approve, reject, comment, or supersede their prior review. A release candidate may reuse regions from earlier candidates. Determine release readiness under a supplied policy, explain every blocking or stale approval, show the ancestry of each region, compare candidates, and export a self-contained ZIP dossier with deterministic member names and timestamps. Changing a region must stale only reviews whose scope included it.

Executable acceptance contract: Use `hashlib`, `io.BytesIO`, and `zipfile`; build candidates reusing/changing regions, assert scoped staleness, superseded review behavior, policy explanation, region ancestry, diff, byte-for-byte deterministic ZIP, fixed `ZipInfo.date_time`, manifest checksum verification, and no readiness mutation during export. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API/data-format contract: `assess(candidate, reviews, policy, prior_candidates) -> dict`, `compare(a, b) -> dict`, and `export_dossier(candidate, reviews, policy, prior_candidates) -> bytes`. Inputs are JSON-shaped snapshots. A candidate is `{id,based_on,regions}` where `based_on` is a prior candidate ID or null and each region is `{text_claims,colors,images,checksum}`. The supplied checksum must equal lowercase SHA-256 of compact sorted-key JSON of the other three fields. A review submission is `{id,candidate,department,decision,scope,comment,supersedes}` with decision `approve|reject|comment`; scope is a sorted list of region names, and supersedes is a prior review ID or null. Policy has `{required_departments,required_regions}`. `prior_candidates` maps IDs to complete candidate snapshots. `assess` returns `{ready,blockers,stale,superseded,ancestry}` with sorted lists. The latest valid superseding submission from a department controls; superseded IDs are reported. An approval remains usable on a later candidate for the regions in its scope that are byte-for-byte unchanged through the supplied candidate lineage, and becomes stale only for scoped regions that changed. Each required department needs usable approval coverage of every required region. Blockers use `DEPT missing approval`, `DEPT rejected: COMMENT`, or `DEPT approval lacks REGION`; stale entries use `REVIEW stale: REGION`. `ancestry` is a sorted list with one plain-language line per current region: `REGION: introduced in ID`, `REGION: unchanged from ID through ID`, or `REGION: changed in ID (previous ID)`. It is an explanatory report derived by comparing snapshots; no region carries an ancestry key or identity derived from content. `compare` returns sorted `{added,removed,changed,unchanged}` region names, comparing complete region content and checksum. Export returns a stored ZIP with members `candidate.json`, `reviews.json`, `readiness.json`, and `checksums.json` in that order. JSON is compact sorted-key UTF-8. Each `ZipInfo.date_time` is `(1980,1,1,0,0,0)` and `create_system` is 0 and `external_attr` is `0o600 << 16`. `checksums.json` maps the other three names to SHA-256 digests. Export is byte-for-byte deterministic and does not mutate input or readiness. The contract does not prescribe how snapshots, reuse, staleness, supersession, or review scope are represented internally.
notes: Revised around complete candidate snapshots and review submissions. Tests cover observable checksum validation consequences, scoped freshness, supersession, readiness explanations, prose ancestry, comparison, deterministic ZIP checksums, and purity.
leakage_self_audit: No forbidden term occurs. Inputs are ordinary full snapshots and review submissions, not region identities, region lineage pointers, or review checksum records. The prose ancestry report and ZIP checksum file are observable requirements, while internal reuse, freshness, and approval organization remain unconstrained.

contract:
Implement `garden.py`. Record beds, crops, families, planting windows, harvest windows, incompatible neighbors, required predecessor crops, volunteer accessibility needs, and seasonal observations such as a bed becoming unavailable. Given a proposed season, report all issues, produce chronological work cards, volunteer-specific views, a bed calendar, and a next-season draft that preserves explicit gardener choices and marks every automatic change. A proposal with issues must still be inspectable and printable.

Executable acceptance contract: Fixed `date` fixture checks overlapping occupancy, neighbor conflict, predecessor absence, inaccessible assignment, closure observation, complete issue aggregation, consistent work-card/bed/volunteer views, next-season preservation of locked choice, marked automatic shifts, and deterministic outputs after permuting input mappings. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (frozen):
`garden.py` must export `plan_season(proposal, observations, next_season_start)`. All arguments and the returned value use only ordinary Python dictionaries, lists, strings, booleans, and `datetime.date` values. The function must not mutate its arguments.

`proposal` has keys `beds` (mapping bed id to `{"neighbors": [bed ids], "accessible": bool}`), `crops` (mapping crop id to `{"family": str, "plant": [date,date], "harvest": [date,date], "incompatible_families": [str], "required_predecessor": str or None}`), `assignments` (list of `{"id": str, "bed": str, "crop": str, "plant": date, "harvest": date, "volunteer": str, "locked": bool}`), `volunteers` (mapping volunteer id to `{"needs_accessible": bool}`), and `previous_crops` (mapping bed id to a list of crop ids, most recent last). `observations` is a list of `{"kind": "bed_unavailable", "bed": str, "start": date, "end": date}`. `next_season_start` is a date.

The result is a dictionary with exactly these top-level keys: `issues`, `work_cards`, `volunteer_views`, `bed_calendar`, `next_season`. Issues are dictionaries `{"code": str, "assignments": [assignment ids], "bed": str}`. Required codes are `OCCUPANCY_OVERLAP`, `NEIGHBOR_CONFLICT`, `PREDECESSOR_MISSING`, `INACCESSIBLE_ASSIGNMENT`, `BED_UNAVAILABLE`, `OUTSIDE_PLANTING_WINDOW`, and `OUTSIDE_HARVEST_WINDOW`; every applicable issue is returned, sorted by `(code, bed, assignments)`. Within every issue, assignment ids are sorted. For a two-bed neighbor issue, `bed` is the lexicographically smaller bed id; otherwise it is the affected bed. Date intervals are inclusive. An assignment outside its crop's inclusive harvest window produces `OUTSIDE_HARVEST_WINDOW`. A neighbor conflict exists when assignments in neighboring beds have overlapping inclusive plant-through-harvest intervals and either crop lists the other's family as incompatible. An overlap is two assignments in the same bed with intersecting intervals. A predecessor requirement is met only when the required crop id occurs in that bed's `previous_crops`.

`work_cards` contains two cards per assignment, `{"date": date, "kind": "plant" or "harvest", "assignment": id, "bed": id, "volunteer": id}`, sorted by `(date, kind, assignment)`. `volunteer_views` maps every volunteer id to that volunteer's cards in the same order. `bed_calendar` maps every bed id to its assignments as `{"assignment": id, "crop": id, "start": date, "end": date}`, sorted by `(start,end,assignment)`. These views are produced even when issues exist.

`next_season` is a list with one entry per assignment, in assignment-id order. Each entry is `{"assignment": id, "bed": id, "crop": id, "plant": date, "harvest": date, "volunteer": id, "locked": bool, "automatic_changes": [str]}`. Locked entries preserve all explicit assignment values and have an empty change list. For an unlocked entry, shift both dates forward by the whole-year offset from the proposal's earliest planting year to `next_season_start.year` (using `date.replace`, and February 29 becomes February 28 if needed), preserving bed, crop, and volunteer; its change list is `['plant','harvest']` if either shifted date differs and otherwise empty. Mapping insertion order must not affect the result.
notes: Uses one fixed date fixture with simultaneous independent faults, verifies complete aggregation, inclusive conflicts, all materialized views, choice preservation, marked shifts, input immutability, and mapping-order determinism.
leakage_self_audit: The appendix names only records, date interval semantics, diagnostics, sorting, and returned reports. It does not prescribe internal representations, rule evaluation architecture, shared intermediate forms, or how the reports are derived.

contract:
Represent workspaces containing sections, notes, references, and nested groups. Clients must be able to obtain total word count, collect unresolved marker identifiers, render a deterministic indented outline, move an item between valid locations, and reject moves that would create invalid containment without altering the workspace. Notes and references may differ in how they contribute to summaries. Tests must construct everything in memory and use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (frozen):
The module must export `Workspace(data)`. `data` is a dictionary `{"title": str, "items": list}` and is deep-copied. Each item has a unique string `id`, a `kind`, and a `title`. A `section` or `group` also has `items`; a `note` has `text`; a `reference` has `label`, `word_count` (a nonnegative integer), and `unresolved` (a list of marker strings). Only workspaces, sections, and groups are valid containers. Marker tokens in note text have the exact form `[[?identifier]]`. Words in note text are maximal runs matched by `\b\w+\b`; marker syntax and its identifier do not count as words. A reference contributes its declared `word_count`.

A workspace provides `total_word_count() -> int`, `unresolved_markers() -> list[str]` (unique identifiers sorted lexicographically), `outline() -> str`, `move(item_id, destination_id, index=None) -> None`, and `to_data() -> dict`. The outline begins with the workspace title, then one line per item in list order; an item's line is two spaces per nesting level followed by `"<kind>: <title>"`. `destination_id` may be the literal `"workspace"` or the id of a section/group. `index=None` appends; otherwise it is a valid Python insertion index from 0 through the destination length. Missing ids, non-container destinations, out-of-range indices, moving a container into itself or anything it contains, and non-string ids raise `ValueError`. Any failed move leaves `to_data()` exactly unchanged. A successful move preserves the item and its descendants and changes only its location/order. `to_data()` returns a deep copy.
notes: Covers deep nesting, both summary contribution rules, marker de-duplication, exact outline formatting, successful relocation, defensive copies, cycle/non-container/missing/index/type failures, and atomic rollback.
leakage_self_audit: The appendix specifies the externally required nested data syntax and workspace operations only. It does not require a shared item abstraction, inheritance, polymorphic traversal, or any particular internal object organization.

contract:
Provide objects that turn a message record into text. Optional capabilities must include adding a subject block, redacting configured fields, appending a legal notice, and recording rendering metadata. Capabilities may be combined in any order, duplicate application must have documented deterministic behavior, and the original message record must remain unchanged. Existing capabilities must work with user-supplied renderers satisfying the public rendering contract. Tests must use only unittest and the standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (frozen):
The module must export `present(message, renderer, capabilities)`. `message` is a mapping and must not be mutated. `renderer` is any user-supplied object with `render(message) -> str`. `capabilities` is a sequence of dictionaries. Supported forms are `{"kind":"subject", "text": str}`, `{"kind":"redact", "fields": [str,...]}`, `{"kind":"legal", "text": str}`, and `{"kind":"metadata", "key": str, "value": JSON-compatible value}`. Unknown kinds or malformed entries raise `ValueError` without calling the renderer.

`present` returns `Presentation(text, metadata)`, where `Presentation` is an exported frozen dataclass with public `text: str` and `metadata: dict`. Processing is deterministic and independent of capability ordering: all configured fields are replaced in a shallow copy of the message by the literal string `[REDACTED]` before exactly one renderer call; distinct subject texts are sorted and prepended as lines `Subject: <text>`; distinct legal texts are sorted and appended as lines; metadata keys are returned sorted by key. Repeating an identical subject, legal text, redacted field, or identical metadata key/value has no further effect. Conflicting values for the same metadata key raise `ValueError` without calling the renderer. Subject and legal sections are separated from the rendered body by one newline, and absent sections add no newline. Redaction applies only to the mapping handed to the renderer, not to text added by the other capabilities.
notes: Uses unrelated user renderers, verifies one render call, field redaction on a copy, order independence, duplicate idempotence, deterministic text/metadata, frozen result, and prevalidation with zero calls.
leakage_self_audit: The appendix exposes a single batch function, renderer protocol, declarative capability records, and result. It does not prescribe capability objects around renderers, delegation topology, or an incremental composition implementation.

contract:
Provide an exhibit record supporting proposals to reserve, install, open, close, maintain, and retire it. The same proposal may be accepted or rejected depending on prior accepted proposals. Each result must report whether it was accepted, a stable reason code, the resulting public status, and any emitted operational notices. Rejected proposals must leave the record unchanged, and a supplied clock must make timestamps deterministic. Tests must use unittest and standard-library fakes only. Use only the Python standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (frozen):
The module must export `Exhibit(exhibit_id, clock)` and a frozen dataclass `ProposalResult` with fields `accepted: bool`, `reason: str`, `status: str`, `notices: tuple`, and `timestamp: datetime.datetime | None`. `clock` is any zero-argument callable returning a `datetime.datetime`. An exhibit starts with public `status == "draft"` and public `history == ()`. `propose(action)` accepts one of the strings `reserve`, `install`, `open`, `close`, `maintain`, and `retire`; an unknown action raises `ValueError` without changing the record or calling the clock.

Accepted actions by public status are: draft→reserve→reserved; reserved→install→installed; installed→open→open; open→close→closed; closed→open→open; closed→maintain→maintenance; maintenance→open→open; and any status other than retired→retire→retired. Any other proposal is rejected. Accepted results use reason `ACCEPTED`, the new status, notices exactly `("<ACTION>:<exhibit_id>",)` where ACTION is upper-case, and one timestamp obtained from the clock. Rejected results use reason `INVALID_FROM_<STATUS>` (both substituted values upper-case), retain the current status, have no notices, use timestamp `None`, do not call the clock, and leave all record data unchanged. On acceptance, append the returned result to `history`; `history` is always a tuple. Repeating the same action is a new proposal governed by the then-current status.
notes: Exercises rejection plus the main path, reopening and maintenance, retirement and repeated retirement, timestamps/call counts, result/history shapes, stable reason codes, and unknown-action atomicity.
leakage_self_audit: The appendix is an explicit black-box action/status table needed for stable acceptance. It requires only one exhibit API and does not prescribe lifecycle helper objects, dispatch structure, or internal transition representation.

contract:
Provide a console-oriented component that accepts structured check-in actions, maintains patient-facing session data, and emits deterministic screen descriptions containing prompts, messages, and selectable choices. It must support beginning a session, recording contact confirmation, choosing an appointment, correcting prior input, and completing or abandoning check-in. Invalid actions must produce an explanatory screen without corrupting accepted data. Input acquisition and output display must be replaceable by unittest fakes using only the standard library.

Public API and data-format contract (frozen):
The module must export `CheckInConsole(appointments, action_source=None, screen_sink=None)`. `appointments` is a sequence of dictionaries with unique string `id` and string `label`; it is copied. Public `session` is a dictionary with exactly `active`, `contact_confirmed`, `appointment_id`, and `completed`, initially `False`, `None`, `None`, `False`. `handle(action) -> dict` accepts a dictionary whose `type` is one of `begin`, `confirm_contact`, `choose_appointment`, `correct`, `complete`, or `abandon`. The latter fields are: `confirmed: bool` for contact, `appointment_id: str` for choice, and `field` plus `value` for correction, where field is `contact_confirmed` (boolean value) or `appointment_id` (known id or None).

A screen dictionary has exactly `prompt: str`, `messages: list[str]`, and `choices: list[dict]`; choices use `{"id": str, "label": str}` in appointment input order. `begin` is accepted only when inactive and starts a clean session. Contact and appointment actions require an active, incomplete session. `complete` additionally requires confirmed contact and a selected appointment; it marks completed and inactive. `abandon` requires an active session and resets to the initial session. Valid correction requires an active incomplete session. Invalid or malformed actions return a screen whose first message begins `Error:`, do not change accepted session data, and do not raise.

After an accepted begin/contact/correction the prompt is respectively `Confirm contact`, `Choose appointment` (if confirmed, otherwise `Confirm contact`), or the next unmet prompt. After a choice it is `Review and complete`; after completion `Check-in complete`; after abandon `Session abandoned`. Appointment choices are present exactly when the prompt is `Choose appointment`, otherwise empty. Accepted screens have an empty messages list except completion yields `["Checked in"]` and abandon yields `["Check-in abandoned"]`.

`run_once()` requires the supplied source and sink, obtains one action by calling `action_source.read_action()`, passes it to `handle`, calls `screen_sink.display(screen)` exactly once, and returns that same screen object. Missing source or sink raises `RuntimeError` before either is called.
notes: Exercises invalid-before-begin behavior, full check-in, selection error rollback, correction, completion, abandonment reset, malformed input, appointment order, and fake source/sink interaction.
leakage_self_audit: The appendix specifies the console boundary, session fields, action/screen dictionaries, and fakeable I/O ports. It does not assign architectural roles or prescribe internal collaboration, notification, or rendering structure.
